strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of gaps in existing multimodal benchmarks (MMSearch) where shallow workflows solve questions without genuine multimodal reasoning
Novel Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation methodology that is principled, well-motivated, and clearly designed to require fine-grained visual reasoning over sparse localized cues
Comprehensive benchmark construction with balanced categories (8 primary, 43 secondary), adversarial filtering procedures, and careful quality control
Thorough evaluation framework with multiple search modes, model-agnostic design, and reproducibility optimizations (result caching, detailed implementation specs)

Insightful analysis including detailed error taxonomy with manual annotation (11 categories), behavioral observations about model differences, and trajectory statistics showing differences between correct/incorrect reasoning
Strong empirical results demonstrating substantial performance gaps (o3: 36% with rollout, Qwen: 6.1%) that validate benchmark difficulty
Excellent presentation quality with clear figures, comprehensive appendices, and well-structured methodology sections
Addresses realistic multimodal information-seeking scenarios with provenance verification requirements under retrieval noise
weaknesses: Relatively small dataset scale (311 tasks) with limited justification; some categories have as few as 17 items (Music), raising concerns about evaluation robustness and long-term utility

Circular difficulty definition where 'Easy' vs 'Hard' labels depend on whether o3 or Gemini can solve without search, creating calibration to specific models' capabilities rather than objective difficulty

Critical unresolved limitation: enabling agent-driven image cropping 'frequently deteriorates performance,' suggesting either misalignment between benchmark design and model capabilities or poor tool implementation, undermining claims about fine-grained visual reasoning

No ablation study validating that Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation is more effective than baseline curation; no comparison of MMSearch vs MMSearch-Plus on same models to quantify actual difficulty increase
Limited model diversity with only one open-source model (Qwen) evaluated; no specialized agents or fine-tuned models tested; Qwen produces 421 invalid tool calls on 45 tasks with unclear impact
Concurrent work (MM-BrowseComp, BrowseComp-VL) addresses similar goals with comparable feature sets (Table 2), making relative contribution and differentiation unclear
Lack of human baseline performance for calibration; no inter-rater agreement reported for manual error annotations or construction quality; answer validation relies solely on LLM-as-a-judge

Limited scope and coverage: underrepresentation of non-English and low-visual-density content; videos/dynamic interfaces acknowledged as underexplored (1.5% of errors require video understanding); narrow domain focus (sports, vlogs, academia)
Only accuracy metric reported without partial credit or semantic similarity measures; no confidence intervals or significance testing despite small category sizes (e.g., n=17)
Search framework limitations: SerpApi may not reflect real search engines; caching assumption that 'top results are stable' needs validation; no generalization to other search engines

strengths: Well-motivated problem statement: Clear articulation that existing multimodal benchmarks can be solved via shallow workflows without genuine multimodal reasoning
Comprehensive evaluation: Systematic evaluation of multiple models (o3, GPT-5, Gemini, Qwen) across three search modes with consistent implementation
Detailed analysis: Error taxonomy, trajectory statistics, and qualitative observations demonstrate solid empirical practice; identification of high-frequency failure modes is useful
Clear presentation: Effective examples and visualizations; well-written throughout
Practical contribution: Model-agnostic search agent framework with browsing tools
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation is sensible but not substantially novel; concurrent work (BrowseComp-VL, MM-BrowseComp) covers similar ground, significantly reducing novelty claim

Misalignment between claims and evidence: Paper claims to test fine-grained multimodal reasoning, but error analysis shows 62.6% of failures are retrieval ('no relevant information found' 51.1%) or hallucination (11.5%), not multimodal reasoning failures (only 15.3% combine 'key information not extracted' and 'relevance not verified')

Weak evidence for multimodal specificity: Authors acknowledge that enabling image cropping 'frequently deteriorates performance,' directly contradicting claims about fine-grained visual reasoning; cropping experiments excluded from main results, suggesting benchmark may not effectively require visual grounding

Problematic Easy/Hard split: Definition (Easy = answerable by o3/Gemini without search) is model-dependent and circular; o3 achieves 50% on 'Easy' split without search, raising questions about filtering effectiveness

Insufficient filtering validation: Adversarial filtering procedure inadequately documented; no quantitative evaluation of effectiveness; no inter-annotator agreement for question design or ground truth annotation

Modest benchmark scale: 311 items is relatively small; unbalanced category distribution (Geography 20.6% vs. Music 5.5%); many categories <40 items with unreliable conclusions; no human baseline for absolute difficulty assessment

Evaluation rigor gaps: No confidence intervals or significance testing; LLM-as-judge may have reproducibility issues with future models; inconsistent search budgets (Qwen capped at 10 rounds, others at 20); search result caching reduces real-world challenge

Weak open-source evaluation: Only Qwen-2.5-VL evaluated; achieves 0% without search, 6.1% with rollout; 45 invalid tool calls (14.5% of tasks) confound understanding with tool-use reliability; limits generalizability
Unstable setup for some models: Qwen regresses under rollout (13.5% → 6.1%), potentially indicating benchmark over-fits to o3's search strategy rather than being fundamentally hard

Reproducibility concerns: Reliance on SerpApi means results could drift; no code/data availability statement; vague implementation details (content extraction/summarization); heavy dependence on online search stability

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: existing multimodal benchmarks solvable via shallow workflows without true multimodal reasoning
Principled Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation methodology for systematic creation of hard questions requiring fine-grained visual signal extraction and out-of-image inference
Comprehensive evaluation across closed-source (o3, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and open-source (Qwen) models with three complementary search modes
Thorough error analysis with systematic taxonomy, trajectory statistics, and representative case studies revealing key failure modes
Carefully curated dataset with adversarial filtering across 8 balanced categories demonstrating genuine difficulty (36% best performance)
Strong empirical findings showing substantial performance gaps and clear headroom for future improvements
Good reproducibility with model-agnostic framework, cached results, and comprehensive appendix statistics
Clear positioning relative to concurrent benchmarks (BrowseComp-VL, MM-BrowseComp)
weaknesses: Moderate dataset scale (311 tasks) relative to typical VQA benchmarks; smaller than some comparable web browsing benchmarks
Limited scope: explicit focus on image-text browsing; videos, interactive systems, and multi-language settings deferred as future work
Incomplete experiments: sub-image cropping disabled with minimal investigation into failure modes; different search budgets across models (20 vs 10 rounds) complicate fair comparison
Error analysis performed only on Gemini-2.5-Pro, not across all evaluated models, limiting generalizability of findings
Missing human baseline and direct quantitative difficulty comparison with BrowseComp despite explicit claims of parity
Easy/Hard split definition is model-dependent (relative to o3/Gemini); adversarial filtering uses subjective criteria with unclear inter-annotator agreement
Limited conceptual novelty: contributions primarily engineering-focused with relatively standard agent framework; Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation is intuitive rather than novel
Unclear dataset release plans and incomplete project information; presentation dense with some implementation details underspecified
Data biases from public web sources acknowledged but not systematically addressed; non-English and low-visual-density pages underrepresented

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clearly articulates gap in existing multimodal browsing benchmarks that rely too heavily on text-only solutions
Principled Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation methodology: Thoughtful approach to creating questions requiring inference of out-of-image facts from visual/temporal cues
Comprehensive multi-model evaluation: Systematic evaluation across closed-source (o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-4o) and open-source (Qwen) models with multiple search modes
Detailed error analysis: Useful taxonomy of failure modes (51.1% no relevant information, 11.5% hallucination) providing insights into model limitations
Good reproducibility documentation: Ethics statement, promised dataset release, implementation details in appendices, example cases and failure analysis provided
weaknesses: Critical flaw with Easy split: Accuracy does NOT improve with image search in multiple models (e.g., o3: 31.4% text-search vs 30.1% full rollout), contradicting the core claim that visual reasoning is required; only 23 easy cases manually inspected, raising data quality concerns

Extremely limited technical novelty: Benchmark is primarily a curation effort; SoM is existing work (Yang et al. 2023); agent framework is straightforward application of existing tools with no algorithmic innovation
Very small dataset: Only 311 questions across 8 categories with 279 unique images; comparable benchmarks typically contain 1000+ questions, limiting generalizability and statistical reliability

Unexplained extremely low performance: Best model achieves only 36% accuracy on easy split, 26.9% on hard split; no clear explanation for why even labeled easy questions are so difficult or why this isn't a benchmark design issue

Weak baselines and missing critical comparisons: No comparison with other multimodal browsing systems; no ablation studies on agent components; Without-Search baseline is trivial; cannot determine if improvements come from agent framework or tool access

Unclear what is being measured: Conflation of multimodal reasoning, world knowledge, tool use, and search effectiveness; MMSearch-lite analysis on only 239 tasks doesn't clearly separate factors; closed-source models retaining geographic knowledge is unsurprising and uninformative
Poor agent framework effectiveness: Full rollout yields only 3-5% improvements; 15% invalid tool calls (451/3000) in Qwen; suggests fundamental tool-use reliability issues not adequately addressed

Insufficient data quality assurance: No inter-rater reliability scores; minimal manual validation; no annotation consistency analysis; no statistical significance testing; temporal drift risk from iterative curation process

Unresolved circular reasoning on core findings: Authors acknowledge easy-split accuracy doesn't improve with image search but attribute this to models 'skipping necessary searches' without evidence; this is not an adequate explanation and undermines confidence in the benchmark

Lack of sufficient ablation studies and analysis: No ablation on SoM component; no category-wise analysis of which benefit from multimodal reasoning; limited analysis of what makes questions difficult beyond failure taxonomy

strengths: Addresses a critical gap in multimodal benchmarking by requiring genuine fine-grained visual reasoning that cannot be solved via text-only heuristics
Rigorous benchmark construction using Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation with multi-step filtering (cross-validation, adversarial filtering, image perturbation)
Comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models (closed-source and open-source) with systematic testing across multiple search modes and end-to-end performance analysis
Insightful empirical analysis including detailed error taxonomy, tool usage patterns via Markov transitions, and clear identification of why models underuse image search
Practical agent framework with Set-of-Mark module enabling region-level visual reasoning and targeted search operations
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and detailed appendices with example trajectories
Thoughtful ethics statement addressing data sourcing, privacy, licensing, and fairness considerations
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation is intuitive but straightforward; SoM module heavily relies on prior work; search framework uses standard tools
Relatively modest benchmark scale (311 tasks) compared to modern benchmarks; narrow domain focus on web-published game/publisher information rather than diverse multimodal reasoning
Extreme performance gap between closed-source (36%) and open-source models (13.5%) raises concerns about benchmark difficulty and potential overfitting to specific model capabilities

No human performance baseline provided, making it difficult to assess whether difficulty is appropriate or excessive; some error cases suggest challenges stem from retrieval noise rather than multimodal reasoning
Error analysis deeply examines only one model (Gemini-2.5-Pro); some 'good cases' appear straightforward, raising questions about task diversity and difficulty distribution
Evaluation design compromises: varying tool constraints across models (Qwen limited to 10 search rounds), uniform 20-minute timeout regardless of computational efficiency
Limited investigation into fundamental drivers of model performance differences beyond tool availability; unclear generalization to other multimodal reasoning scenarios beyond information-finding
Potential dataset construction biases from manual curation; concerns about temporal dataset drift as models improve; reproducibility challenges for web-sourced content that may change over time
